Triggers.value: The same time of day the event occurred
Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette:
Koa is a 42-year-old electrician who lives with his partner in a quiet suburb. He grew up in a large extended family on an island in the Pacific before moving to the mainland for work, and he still speaks with the soft, careful cadence of someone who learned English as a second language. He came to see me about six months after the assault, though he told me it took him that long to admit he needed to.

The event happened on a late autumn afternoon, around four o'clock. Koa was working alone in the basement of an old commercial building, running conduit along a ceiling joist. He had his back to the door. He heard it swing open and slam against the wall, and before he could turn around, a hand seized his shoulder and spun him. He remembers a face - the man was a former coworker who had been fired weeks earlier, drunk, shouting about something Koa had said to the foreman. What Koa remembers most vividly is not the punch that broke his jaw, but the moments just before: the sound of the door, the grip on his shoulder, the fraction of a second when his mind went blank and his body did not move. He remembers that blankness as a kind of failure. He told me he has tried to replay the sequence a thousand times, but it never connects properly. There is the door slamming, and then there is the man's face, and then there is the pain - and between those snapshots there is nothing, a gap that makes him feel as though he must have frozen, must have done something wrong, must have been the sort of person who just stands there while someone comes at him.

That interpretation has become the lens through which he sees everything now. He is certain that a different kind of man - someone tougher, someone more aware, someone worth protecting - would have heard the footsteps, would have turned in time, would not have been in that basement at that hour in the first place. He told me he has come to believe the event happened to him because of who he is fundamentally: someone passive, someone naive, someone who walks through the world with his guard down and therefore deserves whatever finds him. When he says this, his voice is flat, as though stating an obvious fact. He does not argue when I gently suggest otherwise; he simply waits for me to move on, and I understand that his conviction is not something he feels he needs to defend.

The immediate aftermath was functional in a narrow sense. Koa did not miss a day of work. He went back to the same job site the following week, though he refused to go into the basement. His foreman accommodated him, and over the following months the accommodations quietly multiplied. He stopped taking jobs in buildings he had never worked in before. He told his dispatcher he preferred commercial sites he already knew, and because he was a reliable and skilled electrician, no one pushed back. He stopped agreeing to work late shifts. He began leaving at three thirty every day, regardless of what was still unfinished, because by four o'clock he could feel something in his chest start to lock. He did not explain why. He simply stopped taking those calls. At home, his partner noticed changes. Koa had always been a light drinker, but now he started having two or three beers every evening, and sometimes more on weekends. He told himself it was to unwind, but he knew on some level it was to dull the edge of the afternoon, to push the four o'clock hour past into the blur of evening without having to sit inside it. He also spent more and more time on his phone - scrolling through videos, playing simple puzzle games, anything that filled his attention and left no room for the snapshots to surface. His partner would ask if he wanted to watch a movie, and he would say no, because he had learned that any film with a scene of sudden violence - even a bar fight, even a shove - could send him into a state where his heart pounded and he felt as though the room was not real. He avoided TV news for the same reason. He told me he did not want to see anyone else get hurt, but what he meant, I think, was that he could not afford to have his own hurt re-lit.

His body stays on alert in ways that exhaust him. If someone approaches him from the side and touches his arm to get his attention, he flinches hard, sometimes enough that the other person pulls back apologetically. At work, he has learned to position himself so that no one can come up behind him. On the street, if another pedestrian steps suddenly into his peripheral vision, his shoulders jerk and his breath catches before he can tell his brain it is nothing. He avoids unfamiliar places entirely now - new restaurants, friends' houses he has not been to before, even a hardware store on the other side of town. He told me it is not that he expects to be attacked in those places. It is that he cannot assess the danger, cannot run the mental checklist of exits and sightlines and escape routes, and so he stays where he knows every corner. But the most persistent trigger, the one he cannot avoid, is the sound of doors - any door opening or slamming. At home, when his partner comes in from the garage and the kitchen door swings shut with a soft click, Koa's hands clench and his heart hammers before he can even register that it is just her. At job sites, he has learned to walk past every door with his shoulders tight, and if a coworker lets a metal door slam, Koa has to stop what he is doing, breathe slowly, and pretend he is just checking his tools. He told me the sound does not always bring the full memory, but it brings the feeling - that split second before the assault, the blankness, the sense of something about to happen that he cannot stop. He has come to dread the sound of his own front door at the end of the day, because it means the evening has begun, and the evening means the beer and the phone and the slow erasure of hours.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment with his partner. He had been sitting on the couch in the late afternoon, phone in hand, beer on the table, when he realised he could not remember anything about the past three hours. He had scrolled through video after video, had drunk enough to feel numb, and the time had simply vanished. His partner sat down beside him and asked if he was okay, and Koa looked at her and thought about the future - or rather, he tried to think about the future and found nothing there, no image of himself a year from now, no plan, no desire, no point. It was not sadness, he told me. It was a kind of emptiness where a future should have been. He said he felt as though he was already gone, just waiting for his body to catch up. He agreed to come see me because he did not know what else to do, and because he could see in his partner's face that she was afraid for him. What he hopes, he told me quietly, is that someone can help him find the missing pieces of what happened, so that he might finally understand why he is the person this thing happened to. What he is most afraid of is that the answer is simply that he always was.
